Aggregating Demand

This scene adds three consumers into one demand. Stack their curves together and the market curve appears.

Some properties survive the adding-up. If everyone spends their whole budget, so does the market. Double every price and income together, and demand stays put. Move each person's curve and check for yourself.

For example, three 🧑 classmates buy 🍎 apples. The first buys 2, the second 3, the third 5. Together the class buys 10 apples. If prices and 💰 allowances all double, the count stays the same.

Show proof

When every consumer spends her whole budget (individual Walras' law), the summed aggregate demand spends the whole aggregate wealth too — summation is linear, so the property survives.

Now consumer 1 develops a strong taste for good 1, so a=(0.9,0.2,0.2)a = (0.9, 0.2, 0.2)a=(0.9,0.2,0.2) (wealths unchanged at wi=60w_i = 60wi​=60).

Show by computation that the aggregate demand curve shifts up at p1=1p_1 = 1p1​=1, yet the Walras check still holds exactly.

X1=54+12+12=78,X2=6+48+48=102X_1 = 54 + 12 + 12 = 78, \quad X_2 = 6 + 48 + 48 = 102X1​=54+12+12=78,X2​=6+48+48=102
p⋅X=78+102=180=Wp \cdot X = 78 + 102 = 180 = Wp⋅X=78+102=180=W
Show proof

  1. New individual demands: x1=54,12,12x_1 = 54, 12, 12x1​=54,12,12, so X1=78X_1 = 78X1​=78 — moved from 909090 in the previous example. The aggregate curve is sensitive to the distribution of tastes.

  2. Meanwhile x2=6,48,48x_2 = 6, 48, 48x2​=6,48,48, so X2=102X_2 = 102X2​=102, and total spending is 78+102=180=W78 + 102 = 180 = W78+102=180=W. What consumer 1 added to good 1 spending (+36+36+36) she subtracted from good 2 spending (−36-36−36); total spending stays pinned to total wealth.

  3. The lesson: the "shape" of aggregate demand moves with the distribution of tastes, but the "constraint" p⋅X=Wp \cdot X = Wp⋅X=W never breaks, whatever the distribution.
